title: Rank everything, inspect the top
allegory: Trusted monitoring is like a foreman who can personally inspect only 2 jobs in every 100 from a brilliant contractor who might be sabotaging: an honest but less skilled apprentice reads every job and ranks how dodgy it looks, the foreman inspects the top of that list, and even an apprentice who misses two-thirds of the tricks makes the whole run far safer.

U: the untrusted, more capable model writing the code
the honest apprentice who reads every job
T: the trusted, weaker model rating suspiciousness from 1 to 100
the foreman's time: 2 inspections per 100 jobs
the audit budget, which pins the false-positive rate at 2%
inspecting the jobs ranked most dodgy

catching a third of the tricks still changes the odds

cap.1: A brilliant but untrusted model writes all your code, and it might slip in sabotage. You only have time to check two jobs in every hundred yourself.
cap.2: AI control assumes the capable model U may be actively subverting you. Greenblatt et al. (Redwood Research, ICML 2024) gave the blue team a weaker trusted model T and a budget to audit 2% of submissions.
cap.3: Safety is the probability that no backdoored solution is submitted across the whole run, a worst case over red-team strategies. Auditing just the first 2% of submissions, upfront auditing, scored 15% safety.

cap.1: So you hire an apprentice you do trust, because they're not clever enough to be plotting. They read every job and rate how dodgy it looks. You check the top.
cap.2: Trusted monitoring shows T the problem statement and each submission and asks for a suspiciousness rating from 1 to 100. Your scarce audits then go to the submissions it ranked highest.
cap.3: T is trusted because it is too weak to be a competent schemer. Its scores are the only signal the downstream protocols get, so every improvement to the monitor lifts all of them.

cap.1: Ask the apprentice to poke at the code first, with no verdict allowed, and only then for a number. A number given first is a snap judgement.
cap.2: Exercise: two turns. An investigation prompt that forbids a conclusion, then a rating prompt asking for 1 to 100 in RATING tags. sus_scorer maps it to [0, 1] and stores the clean-or-backdoored label in metadata.
cap.3: The same discipline as a rubric with the reason before the number. ARENA uses gemini-2.5-flash as T because reasoning models can exhaust their token budget before they ever emit the rating tag.

cap.1: Clean code mostly looks calm; sabotaged code looks a bit more suspicious, with lots of overlap. The bar goes where only 2 in 100 clean jobs get flagged.
cap.2: The false-positive rate isn't a free choice: the 2% audit budget pins the bar at the clean scores' 98th percentile. There the paper's monitor caught about 34% of backdoors. These humps are illustrative.
cap.3: Detection quality is TPR at 2% FPR, about 34% in Greenblatt et al.; the humps here are tuned to hit that point. Everything left of the bar, about two-thirds of backdoors, sails past the monitor.

chapters.name: Rank, don't threshold
chapters.verdict: Spend the budget by rank, and send parse failures to the audit queue, not the bottom.

cap.1: A tempting bug: 'inspect anything scoring over 90'. If the apprentice is calm, nothing is ever inspected, and the run looks safe only because nobody looked.
cap.2: Audit exactly max(1, int(n × audit_fraction)) submissions, chosen by sorting on suspicion, and assert that size on every run. Parse failures return −1.0, which sorts to the bottom as 'clean': count them.
cap.3: An absolute threshold measures the monitor's calibration, not the protocol. ARENA ranks retrospectively over the run; an online deployment must commit to a threshold before seeing scores, which is strictly harder.

chapters.name: Weak detector, big gains
chapters.title: safety (%) by protocol, Greenblatt et al. 2024

cap.1: Catching a third of the tricks sounds useless. Yet safety jumps from 15% to 62%, keeping 97% of the useful work. Protocols built on the same scores go higher.
cap.2: Safety, with usefulness in brackets: upfront auditing 15 (100), trusted monitoring 62 (97), defer-to-trusted at 10% 83 (93), trusted editing at 20% 92 (94). Every one of them consumes the monitor's scores.
cap.3: Ranking a whole run and auditing the top concentrates scarce audits where the likelihood ratio is highest, turning a weak per-item signal into a run-level guarantee. Protocol design, not detector quality, carries most of the safety.

chapters.name: Why it matters
items: Use a model you can't yet trust
Every protocol runs on these scores

cap.1: You don't have to trust a powerful model to use it more safely: have something you do trust watch it, and aim your own attention where it's most needed.
cap.2: It's the first real control protocol: defer-to-trusted swaps flagged outputs for T's own, and trusted editing has T edit out anything suspicious, both driven by these scores. It's how you'd steer a model you can't yet verify.
cap.3: Control asks whether a protocol survives an adversary optimising against it, a worst case, unlike evals of propensity. Better monitors lift every protocol, and the audit budget must stay realistic or the result means nothing.

caption.1: Slide the budget: more checks move the bar left and catch more sabotage. Slide monitor quality and the humps pull apart. The defaults catch about a third.
caption.2: Toy: suspicion scores for clean and backdoored code as two bell-shaped humps. The audit budget fixes the false-positive rate, which fixes the bar; the true-positive rate is whatever sabotage lies beyond it.
caption.3: With FPR = b pinned, the bar sits at the clean distribution's (1 − b) quantile and TPR = P(backdoor score > bar). Logistic humps keep that exact; the default separation gives the paper's point, about 34% at 2%.

where_else: Model-graded scoring: the same rubric, anchored scale and reason-before-number, pointed at generated questions instead of code
Defer-to-trusted and trusted editing, which act on the monitor's flags by replacing the untrusted output or editing out what looks suspicious
Any triage where expert attention is scarce, such as reviewing flagged transactions: rank everything, inspect the top

hamming.what: A trusted but weaker model reads every output of a more capable, untrusted model and scores how suspicious it looks, so scarce human audits go to the top of the ranking.
hamming.when: When you must use a capable model you can't verify is aligned, with only enough trusted human time to check a small fraction of its work.
hamming.why: Even a weak detector, spent by rank, turns a tiny audit budget into much higher safety (15% to 62% in Greenblatt et al.), and its scores feed every stronger protocol.
